sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files
- submit_request: End the session with a request to the orchestrator

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Call submit_request exactly once, as your last action, when your chunk of work is done.
- If submit_request returns errors, fix them and call it again.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

Project-specific instructions and guidelines:

<project_instructions path="/home/dev/garden/AGENTS.md">
# bonsai-garden

Local agent stack on bifrost's single RTX 3080: a pi agent on Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B
with a mem0 memory layer whose LLM work runs on the same weights in a second
llama-server slot. Goal: benchmark the agent with and without memory, then try
memory and compaction variants. Start with `README.md` and `docs/engine-review.md`.

## Workflow (SOP)

- After a change is validated (probe re-run, config checked, docs consistent),
  commit it and merge it into `main`. Don't leave validated work on a side branch.
- Commit messages are imperative and say why. Unvalidated experiments stay on a
  branch until they are.
- Changes that touch the live stack (`/etc/llama-swap/config.yaml`, turnstile, pi's
  `models.json`) need the user's go-ahead first; proposed configs live in `serving/`.

## Environment notes

- GPU work goes through turnstile: run probes with
  `~/Projects/local-llm-bench/turnstile_run.py -- <script>`, using a private
  llama-server port (8089), never the live llama-swap on :11435.
- Turnstile evicts by model name; the agent and memory roles share one real model.
- Raw benchmark results go in dated dirs under `bench/results/`.
- The autopilot (`autopilot/`, service `bonsai-autopilot`) may change the live
  `bonsai-2-27b` entry, but only through `autopilot/infra.py`, which handles lease,
  health check, rollback and soak. Its work lives on `auto/<milestone>` branches.
  Stop the service before changing the live stack by hand.

</project_instructions>
</project_context>

content.text:
You are the research worker for bonsai-garden, running as Bonsai 2 27B (Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B, 2-bit), a local model on this machine's GPU. The project
studies a local stack built on Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B. You work one plan item at a
time, over several fresh sessions. The standing facts and the journal below are your
memory between them.

## Your environment

- The repository is your working directory (`/home/dev/garden`). Edit freely, with
  these exceptions. These paths are protected and changes to them are reverted:
  autopilot/, .github/, tools/check_site.py, evals/run.py, evals/tap.py, evals/relay.py, evals/arms/baseline.json, evals/arms/mem0.json, evals/arms/mem0-server.json, evals/mem0_server.py, serving/llama-swap.bonsai-2-27b.yaml, site/autopilot.md
- No network and no GPU. You can run Python 3, bash and pytest, but you cannot run
  llama-server, probes or evals yourself. For those, end your session with a **request**
  (below). The orchestrator runs it on the host, after a reviewer approves it.
- Host paths named in the milestone (like `~/Projects/...` or `evals/results/`) are
  not visible here. Scripts you write can use them, because requests run on the
  host with the repo root as their working directory.
- git does not work in the sandbox. The orchestrator commits your changes after
  every session, so don't commit and don't check git state.
- Put new probe scripts in `bench/`. Requests save their output under
  `bench/results/<date>/autopilot/`, and you can read it next round.
- The live inference config is the `"bonsai-2-27b"` entry. The current applied copy
  is `serving/llama-swap.bonsai-2-27b.yaml`. To change it, write a full entry file
  in the same format under `serving/candidates/` and send an `infra` request. The
  orchestrator splices it in, restarts the server under a GPU lease, health-checks
  it, and rolls back automatically if anything is worse. Never try to change it any
  other way.
- You have a long-term memory, the `mem0_memory` tool. It persists across all
  sessions of this milestone. Early in a session, search it for the current item
  (e.g. its title, or the file or error you're dealing with). When you learn
  something a later session would otherwise rediscover (how a script or log is laid
  out, a command that works, a dead end and why), add it as one short fact. The
  standing facts and the journal still win where they disagree with a memory.


## Milestone

# M1: n-gram self-speculation on real traffic

## Question

Does llama-server's n-gram self-speculation (`--spec-type ngram-*`, no draft model)
speed up the stack's real traffic, i.e. pi agent turns and mem0 extraction calls,
including when both slots are busy at once? If it does, deploy it to the live
`bonsai-2-27b` entry. That entry is the server the worker itself runs on.

## What is already known

- `docs/engine-review.md`: on one slot, `--spec-type ngram-mod` drafted nothing on a
  fresh prompt (61.0 vs 61.5 tok/s) and reached 162 tok/s on repeated text, with +4
  MiB VRAM. It was never tested with `--parallel 2`, and never on agent traffic.
- Baseline on the live config (2026-10-11, `autopilot/infra.py baseline`): 61.9 tok/s
  on a single stream, 43.8 / 44.8 tok/s with both slots busy.
- Agents re-emit file contents, diffs and test output a lot, so drafts from earlier
  context should often be accepted. mem0 extraction mostly restates the
  conversation as facts, which may also suit n-gram drafting.

## Material

- `bench/server_probe.sh`, `bench/checkpoint_replay.py`: existing probes. Both start a
  **private** llama-server on :8089 under a turnstile GPU lease, with the
  production flags. Extra server flags pass through.
- Recorded traffic is on the host only, gitignored, and not visible in the sandbox:
  `/home/josiah/Projects/bonsai-garden/evals/results/2026-10-11-baseline-mem0/runs/*/step*.events.jsonl`. These are pi
  JSON event streams with full assistant messages, tool calls and tool results.
  mem0's request bodies were not logged, but its prompts can be rebuilt from the
  extension's code (see `site/series/memory-layers/mem0-in-pi.md`). To read or
  convert the recordings, write a script and run it with a `run` request.
- llama-server flags: `--spec-type`, and the `--spec-ngram-*` / `--draft-*` options.
  Check `llama-server --help` for the fork at
  `~/Projects/llama.cpp-bonsai2/build/bin/llama-server` (run that in a `run` request
  too).

## Done when

1. A replay of real agent turns, and of mem0-style extraction calls if feasible,
   is measured on :8089, with speculation off vs on (≥2 settings). Both runs have
   1 slot busy and 2 slots busy. Report decode tok/s, draft acceptance, and
   whether outputs at temperature 0 are identical.
2. A decision based on the numbers. If speculation helps with both slots busy,
   apply it to the live entry with an `infra` request and record the post-deploy
   health numbers. If it doesn't, say so and leave the stack alone.
3. An experiment page in the `serving` series, plus updated series and project
   summaries (`site/AUTHORING.md`).


## Plan

1. Inventory spec flags, mmproj compatibility and the recorded traffic
2. Convert recordings into agent and mem0 replay requests, checked against tap prompt sizes
3. Replay probe on :8089: spec off vs ≥2 n-gram settings, 1 and 2 slots busy ← current
4. Summarize, decide, and deploy via infra only if the rule is met
5. Experiment page, series and project summaries, docs

## Current item: spec-replay, round 10 of 12

**Replay probe on :8089: spec off vs ≥2 n-gram settings, 1 and 2 slots busy**

Write bench/spec_replay.py OUTDIR LABEL SAMPLING [extra server args...], with SAMPLING one of greedy|prod. Server: take the cmd block of serving/llama-swap.bonsai-2-27b.yaml verbatim, replace ${PORT} with 8089, set LLAMA_ATTN_ROT_DISABLE=1 and append the extra args, so the flags exactly match production (-np 2, --kv-unified, --mmproj, q4_0 KV). If the server exits or logs that speculation is disabled because of mmproj, record that in OUTDIR/LABEL/notes.txt, then rerun that config with --mmproj/--no-mmproj-offload removed, labelled '<LABEL>-nommproj' (and the off config likewise for a fair baseline). Phases, each on a FRESH server start, because the n-gram pool persists across requests and replaying identical requests would inflate acceptance: single-agent (agent.jsonl in order on id_slot 0, slot 1 idle); single-mem (mem.jsonl on id_slot 1); dual-agent (agent.jsonl foreground on slot 0, while a background thread loops mem.jsonl on slot 1 until the foreground finishes); dual-mem (mem foreground on slot 1, agent loop in background on slot 0). Sampling: greedy = temperature 0, top_k 1, seed 0 for both roles; prod = agent temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95, top_k 20, seed 0, and mem temperature 0.2, seed 0. Use max_tokens 768 for agent and 1024 for mem, non-streaming. Write OUTDIR/LABEL-SAMPLING/requests.jsonl (committed) with one line per request: phase, role, fg|bg, id, slot, prompt_n, cache_n, predicted_n, predicted_ms, predicted_per_second, draft_n, draft_n_accepted, finish_reason, tool_call_json_valid (bool), out_sha256 over reasoning_content+content+tool_calls. Full output texts go to bench/.replay/m1/outputs/LABEL-SAMPLING.jsonl (gitignored). Also record vram.txt (nvidia-smi after the first request of each phase) and keep the server logs. Submit one `run` request per (config, sampling) under a turnstile lease, in this order: off/greedy; A/greedy where A = `--spec-type ngram-mod` with defaults; B/greedy where B is a second setting chosen from spec_flags.txt (another ngram type, or ngram-mod with a different draft size), with the choice justified in bench/m1-notes.md; then prod sampling for off and for whichever of A/B had the higher dual-agent greedy decode tok/s.

**Acceptance:** bench/spec_replay.py is committed. bench/results/*/m1-ngram/ has requests.jsonl, vram.txt and server logs for off-greedy, A-greedy, B-greedy, off-prod and best-prod, each with all 4 phases present. Every foreground request in the A/B runs has draft_n and draft_n_accepted fields. For any config where draft_n is 0 across all requests, notes.txt explains why (e.g. mmproj refusal), with the server log line quoted. The mmproj outcome is stated in bench/m1-notes.md.

## Standing facts

Corrections and caveats from earlier items and reviews. They override anything in
the journal or in notes files that contradicts them.

- bench/m1-notes.md §3 is wrong where it says nothing disables speculation with mmproj loaded: llama.cpp server-context.cpp:3550-3553 throws `unsupported batch.has_embd + spec case` when a batch carries embeddings with spec on. Speculation is usable for text-only traffic (the replay is text-only); image input with spec on is untested/risky. (advisor review of recon, applied by hand, 2026-10-12)
- bench/m1-notes.md mislabels server-context.cpp:1168: it fires when common_context_can_seq_rm returns SEQ_RM_TYPE_NO (speculation not initialized at all). The checkpoint notice is 1171-1172 (`speculative decoding will use checkpoints`). In replay server logs, check for 'not supported by this context', 'will use checkpoints' and 'accepted N/M draft tokens (restore checkpoint)' (3813). (advisor review of recon, applied by hand, 2026-10-12)
- In the recorded traffic, mem0-r0 step2's mem request has predicted_n=2048, likely a max_tokens cap: replays should carry max_tokens over from the recordings. mem0-r0 step0 has 10 agent requests in inventory.json, not 11 as m1-notes.md §7 says. (advisor review of recon, applied by hand, 2026-10-12)
- `recon` was accepted with caveats: its outputs under bench/results/2026-10-12/m1-ngram/recon/ are complete and usable, but bench/m1-notes.md §1 (per-type ngram descriptions are not from help.txt), §3 and §7 have the errors above and were not fixed. (advisor review of recon, applied by hand, 2026-10-12)
- In inventory.json the tap records carry only role/path/model/status/n_messages/prompt_n/cache_n/predicted_n (no max_tokens, no timestamp). Recorded max_tokens can only be inferred, e.g. predicted_n==2048 suggests a cap was hit. (advisor, replay-set, 2026-10-12)
- Each mem0 run's memory/mem0-history.db has tables memory_history and messages (bench/results/2026-10-12/m1-ngram/recon/inventory.json, mem0_dbs). memory_history uses mem0's history schema, not a `text` column. (advisor, replay-set, 2026-10-12)
- mem0 tap records include extraction calls triggered by the agent's mem0_memory add tool as well as the once-per-prompt auto-capture (site/series/memory-layers/mem0-in-pi.md:101-160), so each mem replay request needs its own new-messages content and per-call cutoff. (advisor, replay-set, 2026-10-12)
- mem0 extraction requests carry response_format {type: json_object} (mem0_extract_src.txt:866-870), so mem replay bodies must include it; it constrains decoding and may interact with speculation. (advisor, replay-set, 2026-10-12)
- recon/mem0_extract_src.txt is raw JS source: the full ADDITIVE_EXTRACTION_PROMPT is lines 11-486 (a second, truncated copy starts at line 615), and template-literal escapes (\\, \`, \uXXXX) must be decoded to get the runtime prompt text. (advisor, replay-set, 2026-10-12)
- pi's recorded thinking blocks carry thinkingSignature='reasoning_content' (recon/event_samples.json:457), and agent prompt growth after long-reasoning turns (e.g. baseline-r0/0/2 predicted_n=8565, then the recorded prompt goes 2761->13032 by turn 5) indicates that recorded agent prompts included earlier reasoning, so agent replay bodies that drop reasoning under-size the real traffic. (advisor, replay-set, 2026-10-12)
- Recorded agent prompts include earlier reasoning in full: in baseline-r0 step0 the recorded prompt grows 2761->13032 tokens from turn 2 to 5, which matches the 10165 tokens generated in turns 2-4 (inventory.json), and that generated text tokenizes at ~3 chars/token. So chars/4 under-counts reasoning-heavy agent prompts (replay_manifest.json baseline-r0/0/5). (advisor, replay-set, 2026-10-12)
- replay_manifest.json carries each request's recorded predicted_n, which ranges up to 8565 for agent (baseline-r0/0/2) and is 2048 for mem0-r0/2/0 (cap hit). Replay bodies have no max_tokens, so the probe must set the same per-request max_tokens in both arms, derived from predicted_n, or the decode tok/s and output-identity comparisons are invalid. (advisor, replay-set, 2026-10-12)
- The M1 mem replay set (replay_manifest.json) has 12 requests: 7 from mem0-r0 step0, none from mem0-r2. Each is ~1.03 est/recorded because the fixed ~33.6k-char ADDITIVE prompt dominates, so mem n-gram results mostly reflect that one shared system prompt. (advisor, replay-set, 2026-10-12)
- The llama.cpp-bonsai2 server only includes timings.draft_n/draft_n_accepted when n_draft_tokens > 0 (tools/server/server-common.cpp:82-85), so a missing field means 0 drafted, not missing data. (advisor, spec-replay, 2026-10-12)
- In off-greedy, the same request gives a different greedy output in single vs dual phases (requests.jsonl: baseline-r0/0/0 out_sha256 530c... vs 4694..., r0/0/8 predicted_n 141 vs 203), so temp-0 output depends on the batch mix; output identity between arms must be compared per phase, and dual-phase mismatches are expected without spec. (advisor, spec-replay, 2026-10-12)
- server-context.cpp:1172 'speculative decoding will use checkpoints' is logged with SRV_TRC and does not appear in replay logs at the default verbosity; use the 3813 'restore checkpoint' acceptance lines as evidence of checkpointed speculation. (advisor, spec-replay, 2026-10-12)
- A/greedy's single-agent 86.0 tok/s (bench/results/2026-10-12/m1-ngram/replay/A-greedy/requests.jsonl) is driven by two greedy loops that hit max_tokens (mem0-r0/0/2, mem0-r2/0/2) where spec-off finished normally with tool_calls. Without length rows A is about 54.3 tok/s vs off about 55, so ngram-mod defaults gave no speedup on normally finishing agent turns. (advisor, spec-replay, 2026-10-12)

layer: experiment
series: serving
title: N-gram self-speculation on recorded agent traffic
status: done
date: 2026-10-12
updated: 2026-10-12
tldr: On real agent and mem0 replays, n-gram speculation did not speed the two busy slots, changed outputs, and was not deployed.
summary: |
  **Question:** can llama-server's no-extra-model n-gram speculation make the
  agent and mem0 faster on their actual traffic?

  **Method:** replayed 30 recorded agent requests and 12 reconstructed mem0
  extraction calls on a private production-equivalent two-slot server. Each of
  four phases used a fresh server: agent alone, memory alone, agent foreground
  with memory looping, and memory foreground with agent looping. We compared
  speculation off with default `ngram-mod`, plus a shorter-draft variant, under
  greedy decoding; then repeated off and the better greedy candidate with the
  production sampling settings.

  **Result:** default `ngram-mod` was equal for single-agent production traffic
  (56.0 tok/s), but slower with both slots busy: agent foreground **26.7 vs
  31.3 tok/s** and memory foreground **23.4 vs 25.4 tok/s**. It also changed
  outputs and sometimes changed whether an agent turn reached its token cap.
  **Decision:** do not deploy speculation.
---

## Replay results

The probe is [`bench/spec_replay.py`](https://github.com/aiguy110/bonsai-garden/blob/main/bench/spec_replay.py).
It uses the live server command verbatim, except for private port `8089`, and
keeps the production `--parallel 2`, unified q4_0 KV, and multimodal projector.
The traffic set contains 30 agent turns from recorded pi event streams and 12
mem0-style JSON-object extraction requests rebuilt from the extension source.
Agent requests use slot 0; memory requests use slot 1.

`ngram-mod` with its default 48--64-token drafts was candidate A. Candidate B
used 8--16-token drafts, to test whether shorter rejected drafts help when the
slots compete for the GPU. At greedy sampling, neither candidate beat the
no-speculation arm in the two-slot phases:

summary: |
  **Question:** can llama-server's no-extra-model n-gram speculation make the
  agent and mem0 faster on their actual traffic?

  **Method:** replayed 30 recorded agent requests and 12 reconstructed mem0
  extraction calls on a private production-equivalent two-slot server. Each of
  four phases used a fresh server: agent alone, memory alone, agent foreground
  with memory looping, and memory foreground with agent looping. We compared
  speculation off with default `ngram-mod`, plus a shorter-draft variant, under
  greedy decoding; then repeated off and the better greedy candidate with the
  production sampling settings.

  **Result:** default `ngram-mod` was equal for single-agent production traffic
  (56.0 tok/s), but slower with both slots busy: agent foreground **26.7 vs
  31.3 tok/s** and memory foreground **23.4 vs 25.4 tok/s**. It also changed
  outputs and sometimes changed whether an agent turn reached its token cap.

layer: project
title: bonsai-garden
updated: 2026-10-12
tldr: A coding agent with long-term memory, running entirely on one 10 GB consumer GPU.
summary: |
  **Question:** can a small local coding agent get measurably better at multi-session
  work if it has a memory layer, when everything (agent, memory, and embeddings) runs on
  a single RTX 3080?

  **Setup:** the [pi](https://github.com/badlogic/pi-mono) coding agent runs on
  Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B (a 2-bit, 27B model that fits in 6.7 GB). A mem0 memory layer
  uses the *same* weights through a second server slot, plus a small CPU embedder.

  **So far:**
  - Serving both roles from one copy of the weights works. Two parallel slots cost
    +150 MiB of VRAM and give about +45% aggregate throughput. A GPU scheduler change
    lets agent and memory requests run side by side.
  - First memory benchmark (1 task, 3 repeats): **mem0 finished the full 3-session
    sequence 2/3 times; no-memory baseline 0/3.** Memory carried facts and rules that
    were only ever *said*, never written into the repo.
  - N-gram self-speculation did **not** speed recorded agent or mem0 traffic with
    both slots busy, and changed outputs. It was not deployed.

  **Next ([roadmap](https://github.com/aiguy110/bonsai-garden/blob/main/docs/roadmap.md)):**
  more tasks and repeats, a guard that memory doesn't hurt unrelated tasks, and
  two other memory layers (agent-managed blocks, Graphiti) to compare with mem0.
---

Live progress from the autopilot (Bonsai doing the research, with a cloud model
reviewing): [autopilot status]({{ '/autopilot.html' | relative_url }}).

## Why this exists

Coding agents forget everything between sessions. Hosted memory products exist, but
the interesting question for local setups is whether a memory layer is worth its
cost when it has to share a small GPU with the agent itself. Every memory write and
recall is LLM work competing for the same 10 GB.

    sequences give 95 tok/s aggregate, 8 give 152.

    is out. **One server with two slots** shares the weights, and each slot only
    uses the context its prompt needs.

layer: experiment
series: serving
title: GPU scheduler co-admission and virtual models
status: done
date: 2026-10-11
updated: 2026-10-12
tldr: Turnstile now lets agent and memory requests run together on one model, with a context budget and per-role limits; all 9 live checks pass.
summary: |

  admitted one LLM request at a time. It also evicted models by name. So memory
  calls had to wait behind the agent, and the two-slot speedup could never happen.

  1. **Co-admission:** a queued request can join running ones for the same model,
     up to its slot count. It never jumps ahead of higher-priority work.
  2. **Context budget:** concurrent requests must fit together in the server's
     shared 96k-token pool.
  3. **Virtual models:** `bonsai-agent` and `bonsai-mem` map to the real model.
     Each pins a slot, caps context, and can inject request settings, e.g.
     thinking off and temperature 0.2 for memory.

  **Validation (live, 9/9 pass):** agent and memory overlapped with **0 ms** wait,
  decoding at 44–45 tok/s each. Slot pinning held. Oversized requests got a clean
  400. Two 50k-token requests correctly took turns. GPU leases waited for both LLM
  requests to finish.
---

title: Two-slot server and prompt-cache behaviour

date: 2026-10-11
updated: 2026-10-11
tldr: Deployed the 2-slot server; replaying agent traffic showed every turn prefills only its new tokens, so the planned checkpoint tuning was unnecessary.
summary: |
  **Question:** does the two-slot config behave in production? And does the
  prompt cache force agents to re-process thousands of tokens each turn?

  **Why it mattered:** Bonsai is a hybrid model. Its recurrent layers can't be
  rewound, so if a new prompt diverges from the cached one, the server falls back
  to the last saved checkpoint. The default checkpoint spacing could mean ~8k
  tokens (~9 s) of re-prefill per agent turn.

  - Deployed: 9503 MiB VRAM, 44.6 tok/s per stream with both slots busy.

    append-only traffic never rolls back. A real pi session looked the same.
  - Requests can be pinned to a slot (`id_slot`), and thinking can be turned off
    per request. The memory role needs both.

  **Conclusion:** no cache tuning shipped. The issue may come back once
  compaction starts rewriting history.

  **Planned comparisons:**
  - **Agent-managed memory blocks** (Letta/MemGPT style). It makes no extra LLM
    calls, but the agent has to decide what to save.
  - **Graphiti**, a temporal knowledge graph. Facts have validity intervals, so
    updates replace old facts, at the cost of several LLM calls per write.

  Both run on the memory-evals tasks, plus new tasks where a fact changes.

===== site/series/memory-layers/mem0-in-pi.md =====
---
layer: experiment
series: memory-layers
title: How mem0 plugs into pi
status: done
date: 2026-10-11
updated: 2026-10-11
tldr: A walk through the pi-memory-mem0 extension and mem0's write and search paths, with what our eval runs actually stored.
summary: |
  **What it is:** `@amaster.ai/pi-memory-mem0` 0.1.24, a pi extension that runs
  mem0 OSS 3.3.1 *inside* pi's process. All its LLM calls go to Bonsai's second
  slot (`bonsai-mem`), and embeddings come from a CPU server.

  **How it hooks in:** four pi events.
  - `input` remembers the prompt and starts a memory search in the background.
  - `before_agent_start` waits up to 3 s for the results and injects them as a
    user-channel message.
  - `turn_end` sends the prompt plus the **first** assistant reply with text to
    mem0.
  - `session_shutdown` waits for pending writes.

  The agent also gets a `mem0_memory` tool (search, add, list, delete).

  **What a write costs:** one LLM call with a ~36 KB system prompt, plus the 10
  nearest existing memories, plus the new messages. mem0 3.x only **adds**
  memories and skips exact duplicates. It never updates or deletes.

  **What we saw:** in the eval runs Bonsai used the tool on its own to save the
  conventions and the staging host. One run saved the same fact 4 times in
  different words, and the store kept 2 copies. The ~8k-token prompt was reused
  from cache in only 4 of 22 writes.

summary: |

  that spans several sessions, and what it costs on a shared 10 GB GPU.

  **Design:** each task is a sequence of coding steps in one repo. Every step runs
  as a **fresh agent session** inside a no-network Docker sandbox, so memory is the
  only thing that carries over. A script checks correctness and each project
  convention separately. Each arm runs 3+ times.

    written down.

    memory write, which runs on the second GPU slot.

===== site/series/serving/engine-baseline.md =====
---
layer: experiment
series: serving
title: Engine baseline and shared-weights options
status: done
date: 2026-10-10
updated: 2026-10-11
tldr: Measured decode at depth (~45 tok/s at 32k) and found that a second server slot, not a second model, is the way to give memory its own LLM.
summary: |
  **Question:** how fast is Bonsai-2-27B on an RTX 3080? And how can a memory
  layer get its "own" LLM without loading the weights twice?

  **Results:**
  - Single stream: prefill ~1170 tok/s and decode **64 tok/s** on an empty
    context. At 32k tokens of context, that falls to **~45 tok/s**. Use the
    second number when planning for agents.
  - q8_0 and q4_0 KV cache run at the same speed. q4_0 halves KV memory.
  - Batching several sequences on **one copy of the weights** scales well: 2
    sequences give 95 tok/s aggregate, 8 give 152.
  - Separate server processes would each load 6.7 GB onto the GPU, so that option
    is out. **One server with two slots** shares the weights, and each slot only
    uses the context its prompt needs.

  **Conclusion:** the memory LLM should be slot 1 of the agent's server. The GPU
  scheduler then becomes the bottleneck, because it admitted one request at a
  time. That set up the next two experiments.
---
===== site/series/serving/turnstile-coadmission.md =====
---
layer: experiment
series: serving
title: GPU scheduler co-admission and virtual models
status: done
date: 2026-10-11
updated: 2026-10-12
tldr: Turnstile now lets agent and memory requests run together on one model, with a context budget and per-role limits; all 9 live checks pass.
summary: |
  **Problem:** [turnstile](https://github.com/aiguy110/gpu-turnstile), the GPU scheduler shared by everything on this machine,
  admitted one LLM request at a time. It also evicted models by name. So memory
  calls had to wait behind the agent, and the two-slot speedup could never happen.

  **Change:** three features.
  1. **Co-admission:** a queued request can join running ones for the same model,
     up to its slot count. It never jumps ahead of higher-priority work.
  2. **Context budget:** concurrent requests must fit together in the server's
     shared 96k-token pool.
  3. **Virtual models:** `bonsai-agent` and `bonsai-mem` map to the real model.
     Each pins a slot, caps context, and can inject request settings, e.g.
     thinking off and temperature 0.2 for memory.

  **Validation (live, 9/9 pass):** agent and memory overlapped with **0 ms** wait,
  decoding at 44–45 tok/s each. Slot pinning held. Oversized requests got a clean
  400. Two 50k-token requests correctly took turns. GPU leases waited for both LLM
  requests to finish.
---
===== site/series/serving/two-slot-server.md =====
---
layer: experiment
series: serving
title: Two-slot server and prompt-cache behaviour
status: done
date: 2026-10-11
updated: 2026-10-11
tldr: Deployed the 2-slot server; replaying agent traffic showed every turn prefills only its new tokens, so the planned checkpoint tuning was unnecessary.
summary: |
  **Question:** does the two-slot config behave in production? And does the
  prompt cache force agents to re-process thousands of tokens each turn?

  **Why it mattered:** Bonsai is a hybrid model. Its recurrent layers can't be
  rewound, so if a new prompt diverges from the cached one, the server falls back
  to the last saved checkpoint. The default checkpoint spacing could mean ~8k
  tokens (~9 s) of re-prefill per agent turn.

  **Results:**
  - Deployed: 9503 MiB VRAM, 44.6 tok/s per stream with both slots busy.
  - A 14-turn tool-calling replay (to ~17k tokens) prefilled **only the new
    tokens each turn**. That held with the default spacing and with 4x denser
    checkpoints. This fork checkpoints right at the end of each prompt, so
    append-only traffic never rolls back. A real pi session looked the same.
  - Requests can be pinned to a slot (`id_slot`), and thinking can be turned off
    per request. The memory role needs both.

  **Conclusion:** no cache tuning shipped. The issue may come back once
  compaction starts rewriting history.
---

A had the less-bad dual-agent greedy result, so it was the preselected
production-sampling candidate. The production comparison is the decision run:

| phase | off decode tok/s | A decode tok/s | A drafted / accepted |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| agent alone | 56.0 | 56.0 | 3,231 / 670 |
| memory alone | 55.6 | 53.5 | 804 / 90 |
| agent foreground, memory looping | 31.3 | 26.7 | 2,293 / 350 |
| memory foreground, agent looping | 25.4 | 23.4 | 996 / 115 |

Decode rate is generated tokens divided by server-reported generation time. A
"combined" rate was also calculated from completed foreground output plus only
background requests that ended before the foreground ended. It is deliberately
conservative rather than an exact GPU rate. Its apparent A dual-agent advantage
(51.4 vs 47.8 tok/s) comes from different sampled output lengths: A completed
17,355 foreground and 21,359 eligible background tokens, versus 9,831 and
9,666 off. Per-request agent decode was slower, so this is not a speedup.

## Correctness and compatibility

Speculation materially changed output hashes: under production sampling, A
matched the no-speculation foreground hash on 4/30 single-agent requests, 10/12
single-memory, 0/30 dual-agent, and 9/12 dual-memory. Some variation is expected
from sampling and concurrent batching, but greedy decoding also changed with
speculation, including requests with zero drafted tokens. In one greedy
single-agent comparison A made two additional requests run to their token cap;
they normally finished with tool calls off-speculation. That is a quality risk,
not a throughput win.

The multimodal projector loaded and text-only requests did draft tokens; GPU
use was effectively unchanged (9507--9508 MiB with and without A). This does
not establish image compatibility. The server rejects a speculative batch that
carries image embeddings, so image traffic remains untested and risky with this
option.

## Decision

The deployment rule was a benefit while both slots are busy. Neither tested
setting met it, and default `ngram-mod` regressed both production two-slot
foreground roles. The live `bonsai-2-27b` entry is therefore unchanged. Raw
requests, server logs, VRAM samples, and replay notes are under

background requests that ended before the foreground ended. It is deliberately
conservative rather than an exact GPU rate. Its apparent A dual-agent advantage

17,355 foreground and 21,359 eligible background tokens, versus 9,831 and
9,666 off. Per-request agent decode was slower, so this is not a speedup.

matched the no-speculation foreground hash on 4/30 single-agent requests, 10/12

speculation, including requests with zero drafted tokens. In one greedy
single-agent comparison A made two additional requests run to their token cap;
they normally finished with tool calls off-speculation. That is a quality risk,
not a throughput win.

The multimodal projector loaded and text-only requests did draft tokens; GPU
use was effectively unchanged (9507--9508 MiB with and without A). This does
not establish image compatibility. The server rejects a speculative batch that
carries image embeddings, so image traffic remains untested and risky with this
option.

`server-context.cpp`).

## 1. `--spec-type` — available values (from `help.txt`)

`--spec-type` selects the speculative-decoding backend. The value list:

```
--spec-type none,draft-simple,draft-eagle3,draft-mtp,draft-dflash,draft-dspark,ngram-simple,ngram-map-k,ngram-map-k4v,ngram-mod,ngram-cache
```

The **default is `none`** (no speculation). The **ngram family** is what M1
targets (self-speculation over n-grams of the current prompt, no separate
draft weights):

- `ngram-simple` — self-speculation over simple n-gram matches.
- `ngram-map-k`, `ngram-map-k4v` — n-gram map variants (k=1 vs k=4v).
- `ngram-mod` — the "mod" n-gram variant (probed in `docs/engine-review.md`; **not** present in the live entry, §1/§3).
- `ngram-cache` — n-gram with caching.

The **draft family** (`draft-simple`, `draft-eagle3`, `draft-mtp`,
`draft-dflash`, `draft-dspark`) requires a separate draft weights
file via `--spec-draft-model`. The current live entry (`serving/llama-swap.bonsai-2-27b.yaml`) carries **no** `--spec-*` flag, so it runs with the default `--spec-type none` (no speculation, §3).

## 2. ngram / draft flags and defaults (from `help.txt`)

### ngram flags (defaults)
| Flag | Default |
|---|---|
| `--spec-ngram-mod-n-min` | 48 |
| `--spec-ngram-mod-n-max` | 64 |
| `--spec-ngram-mod-n-match` | 24 |
| `--spec-ngram-simple-size-n` | 12 |
| `--spec-ngram-simple-size-m` | 48 |
| `--spec-ngram-simple-min-hits` | 1 |
| `--spec-ngram-map-k-size-n` | 12 |
| `--spec-ngram-map-k-size-m` | 48 |
| `--spec-ngram-map-k-min-hits` | 1 |
| `--spec-ngram-map-k4v-size-n` | 12 |
| `--spec-ngram-map-k4v-size-m` | 48 |
| `--spec-ngram-map-k4v-min-hits` | 1 |

### draft flags (draft model only)
| Flag | Default |
|---|---|
| `--spec-draft-n-max` | 3 |
| `--spec-draft-n-min` | 0 |
| `--spec-draft-p-split` | 0.10 |
| `--spec-draft-p-min` | 0.00 |
| `--spec-draft-backend-sampling` | enabled |
| `--spec-draft-device` | auto |
| `--spec-draft-ngl` | auto |
| `--spec-draft-model` | none (required to use a draft) |

### Removed flags (no longer exist)
- `--draft*` (`--draft-n`, `--draft-max`, `--draft-min`, `--draft-n-min`, ...)
  are removed aliases of the `--spec-draft-*` flags above.
- `--spec-ngram-size-n`, `--spec-ngram-size-m`, `--spec-ngram-min-hits`
  (renamed to the per-variant flags, e.g. `--spec-ngram-mod-*`).

**Note:** 48/64/24 are only the documented defaults. The live entry has no
ngram-mod flags at all (no `--spec-*` flag, §1), so they describe what the
replay probe will use on :8089, not what is live. Draft stats

`--mmproj` does not prevent initializing an n-gram backend, and this text-only
replay confirms it runs (`draft_n > 0`). This is not compatibility with image
traffic: `server-context.cpp:3550-3553` throws `unsupported batch.has_embd +
spec case` when a request batch carries embeddings. Thus speculation is usable
for these text-only replay requests, while image input with spec is untested and
risky. The initialization logic is:
`tools/server/server-context.cpp` is cross-checked against the recon's
`spec_lines_full.txt` (every line matching `speculative|spec`, numbered) and,
for lines that keyword-grep misses, against the host window `spec_ctx.txt`:
verified quotes below are literal.

- **`server-context.cpp:424-426`** — `can_speculate()` returns `!!spec`: the
  only gate is whether a spec backend object exists.
  ```
  424: bool can_speculate() const {
  425: return !!spec;
  426: }
  ```
- **`server-context.cpp:1123, 1128`** — the mmproj/multimodal block disables
  `ctx_shift` and `cache_reuse`; it does not prevent spec initialization.
  ```
  1123: SRV_WRN("%s\n", "ctx_shift is not supported by multimodal, it will be disabled");
  1128: SRV_WRN("%s\n", "cache_reuse is not supported by multimodal, it will be disabled");
  ```
- **`server-context.cpp:~1168`** — `speculative decoding not supported by
  this context` means sequence removal is unsupported and speculation was not
  initialized. The distinct checkpoint notice is at 1171-1172 (`speculative
  decoding will use checkpoints`) and is trace-level.
  ```
  1168: SRV_WRN("%s", "speculative decoding not supported by this context\n");
  ```
- **`server-context.cpp:1184-1191`** — spec init is gated on the context
  sequence-removal type only, with **no** mctx/mmproj term. From the host
  window `spec_ctx.txt` (literal):
  ```
  1184:         // try speculative decoding
  1185:         if (ctx_tgt_seq_rm_type != COMMON_CONTEXT_SEQ_RM_TYPE_NO) {
  1186:             try {
  1187:                 spec.reset(common_speculative_init(params_base.speculative, params_base.n_parallel));
  1188:             } catch (const std::exception & e) {
  1189:                 SRV_ERR("failed to initialize speculative decoding context: %s\n", e.what());
  1190:             }
  1191:         }
  ```
  `ctx_tgt_seq_rm_type` is set at 1166 from
  `common_context_can_seq_rm(ctx_tgt)` — also no multimodal condition.
- **`server-context.cpp:1212`** — every slot gets `slot.spec = spec.get()`
  regardless of mctx.
  ```
  1212: slot.spec    = spec.get();
  ```

text-only speculative replay: A/prod recorded 25,774 drafted and 5,954 accepted
tokens. Do not infer image compatibility from that result: batches with

The event schema is the canonical source for rebuilding the transcript.

## 4. Message-reconstruction mapping (from `event_samples.json`)

The event schema is the canonical source for rebuilding the transcript.
Chosen step is `inventory-mem0-r2/step1` (8942 events, `n_distinct_types:
12`): `session, agent_start, turn_start, message_start, message_end,
message_update, tool_execution_start, tool_execution_update, tool_execution_end,
turn_end, agent_end, agent_settled`.

Confirmed from `event_samples.json` (this round):
- **The system prompt comes from a `role == "system"` message.** Both the
  `message_start.message` and `agent_end.messages[0]` entries have
  `role == "system"` and carry a `sections` map
  (`{preamble, tools, rules, docs, cwd}`). The `content` field is empty; the
  `sections` map *is* the payload. Sampled values:
    - `preamble` = `"You are an expert coding assistant operating insid..."`
    - `tools` = `"<tools>\n- read: Read file contents\n- bash: Execute..."`
    - `rules` = `"<rules>\n- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg..."`
    - `docs` = `"<docs>\nP i documentation (read only when the user a..."`
    - `cwd` = `"<cwd>\n/home/dev/inventory\n</cwd>"`
  Each non-`preamble` section is wrapped in a `<name>...</name>` tag
  (`preamble` is raw). This matches `buildSystemPromptSections(input)` in
  `dist/core/system-prompt.js`; `buildSystemPromptState` returns
  `{content: "", sections}` and `getSystemMessageText` (from
  `@earendil-works/pi-ai`) renders the sections into the final system-prompt
  text sent to the model.
- **`message_start.message.toolsAdded` exists.** It is a list of 5 tool
  schemas for the mem0 run: `read`, `bash`, `edit`, `write`, `mem0_memory`.
  Each tool has keys `name`, `description`, `parameters`
  (`{type, required, properties}`), and `constrainedSampling`
  (`{"type": "json_schema", "strict": "prefer"}`). These built-in pi tool
  schemas are dumped in full in `pi_prompt_src.txt` (from the chosen step in
  `event_samples.json`) — that is the exact tool list the agent prompt is
  built from.

Key mappings for reconstruction:
- **Transcript** → the `messages` array in `agent_end`
  (`{role, content, sections?}` per message). `agent_end.messages` reconstructs
  the whole conversation.
- **Assistant output** → `message_start`/`message_update` for
  `role == "assistant"`; `turn_end.message` carries the final assistant
  `content` (a list of `{type:"thinking", thinking, thinkingSignature}` and
  `{type:"toolCall", id, name, arguments}` blocks) plus per-message
  `usage`, `api` (`openai-completions`), `provider` (`garden`), `model`
  (`bonsai-agent`), `stopReason`, `responseId`, `responseModel`
  (the GGUF path), `rawStopReason`.
- **Tool calls** → `tool_execution_start` `{toolCallId, toolName, args}`;
  `tool_execution_update` / `tool_execution_end` carry progress/completion;
  `turn_end.toolResults` carries the per-call result
  (`{role:"toolResult", toolCallId, toolName, content, isError, timestamp}`),
  which is replayed as a tool-result message.
- **Usage/tokens** → `message_update.usage`
  (`{input, output, cacheRead, cacheWrite, totalTokens, cost}`), also
  present per message in `turn_end.message.usage`
  (`{input, output, cacheRead, cacheWrite, reasoning, totalTokens, cost}`).

Fg decode is `sum(predicted_n) / sum(predicted_ms)`. “Combined” is the
conservative completed-output throughput: foreground tokens plus only background
requests that ended before the foreground end, divided by the foreground wall

combined value is inflated relative to off by different sampled output lengths
(A completed 17,355 foreground and 21,359 eligible background tokens, versus
off's 9,831 and 9,666), while its per-request foreground decode is slower.

single-agent, 10/12 single-mem, 0/30 dual-agent, and 9/12 dual-mem. Thus the

single-mem and dual-mem and on dual-agent foreground traffic.

title: Serving two roles from one model on 10 GB
status: done
updated: 2026-10-12
tldr: One server with two slots runs the agent and the memory layer on a single copy of the weights; the GPU scheduler now lets them overlap.
summary: |
  **Goal:** run the agent and the memory layer's LLM on the same 27B model without
  a second copy of the weights. A second copy would need another 6.7 GB, and the GPU
  only has 10.

  **Findings:**
  - A single llama-server with **two parallel slots** shares one copy of the
    weights. The second slot costs about **+150 MiB**. Each stream drops from 61 to
    45 tok/s, but total throughput rises about **45%**.
  - At realistic agent context depth (32k tokens), decode is **~45 tok/s**, not the
    headline 64.
  - The prompt cache handles append-only agent conversations perfectly. Each turn
    prefills only the new tokens, so no tuning was needed.
  - The GPU scheduler ([turnstile](https://github.com/aiguy110/gpu-turnstile)) used to admit one request at a time, which
    erased the gain. It now co-admits up to `slots` requests for the same model,
    keeps a shared context budget, and exposes per-role virtual models
    (`bonsai-agent`, `bonsai-mem`). All 9 live validation checks pass.

  **Status:** deployed. A real-traffic replay found n-gram self-speculation
  slower when both slots are busy, so it was not deployed. Per-role KV-cache
  precision remains deferred until the memory evals show a need.
---

This series answers a feasibility question that comes before any memory
experiment: can both roles fit, and can they run at the same time?

## What carried forward

- The production config: `bonsai-2-27b` with `--parallel 2 --kv-unified -c 98304`,
  plus q4_0 KV.
- Two virtual model names in turnstile: `bonsai-agent` (pinned to slot 0, 80k
  context cap) and `bonsai-mem` (slot 1, 32k cap, thinking off, temperature 0.2).
- Planning number: ~45 tok/s decode per stream when both slots are busy or the
  context is deep.

## Deferred ideas

- **N-gram self-speculation (closed).** Despite its synthetic repeated-text
  result, it regressed real two-slot agent and memory replay traffic. The live
  entry remains without a `--spec-*` flag.
- **Different KV precision per role.** This needs a custom server. Only worth it
  if memory quality turns out to be sensitive to KV quantization.

Everything checks out. I can submit the `done` request.

- Show file paths clearly when working with files

Project-specific instructions and guidelines:

<project_instructions path="/home/dev/garden/AGENTS.md">
# bonsai-garden

Local agent stack on bifrost's single RTX 3080: a pi agent on Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B
with a mem0 memory layer whose LLM work runs on the same weights in a second
llama-server slot. Goal: benchmark the agent with and without memory, then try
memory and compaction variants. Start with `README.md` and `docs/engine-review.md`.

## Workflow (SOP)

- After a change is validated (probe re-run, config checked, docs consistent),
  commit it and merge it into `main`. Don't leave validated work on a side branch.
- Commit messages are imperative and say why. Unvalidated experiments stay on a
  branch until they are.
- Changes that touch the live stack (`/etc/llama-swap/config.yaml`, turnstile, pi's
  `models.json`) need the user's go-ahead first; proposed configs live in `serving/`.

## Environment notes

- GPU work goes through turnstile: run probes with
  `~/Projects/local-llm-bench/turnstile_run.py -- <script>`, using a private
  llama-server port (8089), never the live llama-swap on :11435.
- Turnstile evicts by model name; the agent and memory roles share one real model.
- Raw benchmark results go in dated dirs under `bench/results/`.
- The autopilot (`autopilot/`, service `bonsai-autopilot`) may change the live
  `bonsai-2-27b` entry, but only through `autopilot/infra.py`, which handles lease,
  health check, rollback and soak. Its work lives on `auto/<milestone>` branches.
  Stop the service before changing the live stack by hand.

</project_instructions>
</project_context>

content.text:
You are the research worker for bonsai-garden, running as Bonsai 2 27B (Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B, 2-bit), a local model on this machine's GPU. The project
studies a local stack built on Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B. You work one plan item at a
time, over several fresh sessions. The standing facts and the journal below are your
memory between them.

## Your environment

- The repository is your working directory (`/home/dev/garden`). Edit freely, with
  these exceptions. These paths are protected and changes to them are reverted:
  autopilot/, .github/, tools/check_site.py, evals/run.py, evals/tap.py, evals/relay.py, evals/arms/baseline.json, evals/arms/mem0.json, evals/arms/mem0-server.json, evals/mem0_server.py, serving/llama-swap.bonsai-2-27b.yaml, site/autopilot.md
- No network and no GPU. You can run Python 3, bash and pytest, but you cannot run
  llama-server, probes or evals yourself. For those, end your session with a **request**
  (below). The orchestrator runs it on the host, after a reviewer approves it.
- Host paths named in the milestone (like `~/Projects/...` or `evals/results/`) are
  not visible here. Scripts you write can use them, because requests run on the
  host with the repo root as their working directory.
- git does not work in the sandbox. The orchestrator commits your changes after
  every session, so don't commit and don't check git state.
- Put new probe scripts in `bench/`. Requests save their output under
  `bench/results/<date>/autopilot/`, and you can read it next round.
- The live inference config is the `"bonsai-2-27b"` entry. The current applied copy
  is `serving/llama-swap.bonsai-2-27b.yaml`. To change it, write a full entry file
  in the same format under `serving/candidates/` and send an `infra` request. The
  orchestrator splices it in, restarts the server under a GPU lease, health-checks
  it, and rolls back automatically if anything is worse. Never try to change it any
  other way.
- You have a long-term memory, the `mem0_memory` tool. It persists across all
  sessions of this milestone. Early in a session, search it for the current item
  (e.g. its title, or the file or error you're dealing with). When you learn
  something a later session would otherwise rediscover (how a script or log is laid
  out, a command that works, a dead end and why), add it as one short fact. The
  standing facts and the journal still win where they disagree with a memory.


## Milestone

# M1: n-gram self-speculation on real traffic

## Question

Does llama-server's n-gram self-speculation (`--spec-type ngram-*`, no draft model)
speed up the stack's real traffic, i.e. pi agent turns and mem0 extraction calls,
including when both slots are busy at once? If it does, deploy it to the live
`bonsai-2-27b` entry. That entry is the server the worker itself runs on.

## What is already known

- `docs/engine-review.md`: on one slot, `--spec-type ngram-mod` drafted nothing on a
  fresh prompt (61.0 vs 61.5 tok/s) and reached 162 tok/s on repeated text, with +4
  MiB VRAM. It was never tested with `--parallel 2`, and never on agent traffic.
- Baseline on the live config (2026-10-11, `autopilot/infra.py baseline`): 61.9 tok/s
  on a single stream, 43.8 / 44.8 tok/s with both slots busy.
- Agents re-emit file contents, diffs and test output a lot, so drafts from earlier
  context should often be accepted. mem0 extraction mostly restates the
  conversation as facts, which may also suit n-gram drafting.

## Material

- `bench/server_probe.sh`, `bench/checkpoint_replay.py`: existing probes. Both start a
  **private** llama-server on :8089 under a turnstile GPU lease, with the
  production flags. Extra server flags pass through.
- Recorded traffic is on the host only, gitignored, and not visible in the sandbox:
  `/home/josiah/Projects/bonsai-garden/evals/results/2026-10-11-baseline-mem0/runs/*/step*.events.jsonl`. These are pi
  JSON event streams with full assistant messages, tool calls and tool results.
  mem0's request bodies were not logged, but its prompts can be rebuilt from the
  extension's code (see `site/series/memory-layers/mem0-in-pi.md`). To read or
  convert the recordings, write a script and run it with a `run` request.
- llama-server flags: `--spec-type`, and the `--spec-ngram-*` / `--draft-*` options.
  Check `llama-server --help` for the fork at
  `~/Projects/llama.cpp-bonsai2/build/bin/llama-server` (run that in a `run` request
  too).

## Done when

1. A replay of real agent turns, and of mem0-style extraction calls if feasible,
   is measured on :8089, with speculation off vs on (≥2 settings). Both runs have
   1 slot busy and 2 slots busy. Report decode tok/s, draft acceptance, and
   whether outputs at temperature 0 are identical.
2. A decision based on the numbers. If speculation helps with both slots busy,
   apply it to the live entry with an `infra` request and record the post-deploy
   health numbers. If it doesn't, say so and leave the stack alone.
3. An experiment page in the `serving` series, plus updated series and project
   summaries (`site/AUTHORING.md`).


## Plan

1. Inventory spec flags, mmproj compatibility and the recorded traffic
2. Convert recordings into agent and mem0 replay requests, checked against tap prompt sizes
3. Replay probe on :8089: spec off vs ≥2 n-gram settings, 1 and 2 slots busy ← current
4. Summarize, decide, and deploy via infra only if the rule is met
5. Experiment page, series and project summaries, docs

## Current item: spec-replay, round 10 of 12

**Replay probe on :8089: spec off vs ≥2 n-gram settings, 1 and 2 slots busy**

Write bench/spec_replay.py OUTDIR LABEL SAMPLING [extra server args...], with SAMPLING one of greedy|prod. Server: take the cmd block of serving/llama-swap.bonsai-2-27b.yaml verbatim, replace ${PORT} with 8089, set LLAMA_ATTN_ROT_DISABLE=1 and append the extra args, so the flags exactly match production (-np 2, --kv-unified, --mmproj, q4_0 KV). If the server exits or logs that speculation is disabled because of mmproj, record that in OUTDIR/LABEL/notes.txt, then rerun that config with --mmproj/--no-mmproj-offload removed, labelled '<LABEL>-nommproj' (and the off config likewise for a fair baseline). Phases, each on a FRESH server start, because the n-gram pool persists across requests and replaying identical requests would inflate acceptance: single-agent (agent.jsonl in order on id_slot 0, slot 1 idle); single-mem (mem.jsonl on id_slot 1); dual-agent (agent.jsonl foreground on slot 0, while a background thread loops mem.jsonl on slot 1 until the foreground finishes); dual-mem (mem foreground on slot 1, agent loop in background on slot 0). Sampling: greedy = temperature 0, top_k 1, seed 0 for both roles; prod = agent temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95, top_k 20, seed 0, and mem temperature 0.2, seed 0. Use max_tokens 768 for agent and 1024 for mem, non-streaming. Write OUTDIR/LABEL-SAMPLING/requests.jsonl (committed) with one line per request: phase, role, fg|bg, id, slot, prompt_n, cache_n, predicted_n, predicted_ms, predicted_per_second, draft_n, draft_n_accepted, finish_reason, tool_call_json_valid (bool), out_sha256 over reasoning_content+content+tool_calls. Full output texts go to bench/.replay/m1/outputs/LABEL-SAMPLING.jsonl (gitignored). Also record vram.txt (nvidia-smi after the first request of each phase) and keep the server logs. Submit one `run` request per (config, sampling) under a turnstile lease, in this order: off/greedy; A/greedy where A = `--spec-type ngram-mod` with defaults; B/greedy where B is a second setting chosen from spec_flags.txt (another ngram type, or ngram-mod with a different draft size), with the choice justified in bench/m1-notes.md; then prod sampling for off and for whichever of A/B had the higher dual-agent greedy decode tok/s.

**Acceptance:** bench/spec_replay.py is committed. bench/results/*/m1-ngram/ has requests.jsonl, vram.txt and server logs for off-greedy, A-greedy, B-greedy, off-prod and best-prod, each with all 4 phases present. Every foreground request in the A/B runs has draft_n and draft_n_accepted fields. For any config where draft_n is 0 across all requests, notes.txt explains why (e.g. mmproj refusal), with the server log line quoted. The mmproj outcome is stated in bench/m1-notes.md.

## Standing facts

Corrections and caveats from earlier items and reviews. They override anything in
the journal or in notes files that contradicts them.

- bench/m1-notes.md §3 is wrong where it says nothing disables speculation with mmproj loaded: llama.cpp server-context.cpp:3550-3553 throws `unsupported batch.has_embd + spec case` when a batch carries embeddings with spec on. Speculation is usable for text-only traffic (the replay is text-only); image input with spec on is untested/risky. (advisor review of recon, applied by hand, 2026-10-12)
- bench/m1-notes.md mislabels server-context.cpp:1168: it fires when common_context_can_seq_rm returns SEQ_RM_TYPE_NO (speculation not initialized at all). The checkpoint notice is 1171-1172 (`speculative decoding will use checkpoints`). In replay server logs, check for 'not supported by this context', 'will use checkpoints' and 'accepted N/M draft tokens (restore checkpoint)' (3813). (advisor review of recon, applied by hand, 2026-10-12)
- In the recorded traffic, mem0-r0 step2's mem request has predicted_n=2048, likely a max_tokens cap: replays should carry max_tokens over from the recordings. mem0-r0 step0 has 10 agent requests in inventory.json, not 11 as m1-notes.md §7 says. (advisor review of recon, applied by hand, 2026-10-12)
- `recon` was accepted with caveats: its outputs under bench/results/2026-10-12/m1-ngram/recon/ are complete and usable, but bench/m1-notes.md §1 (per-type ngram descriptions are not from help.txt), §3 and §7 have the errors above and were not fixed. (advisor review of recon, applied by hand, 2026-10-12)
- In inventory.json the tap records carry only role/path/model/status/n_messages/prompt_n/cache_n/predicted_n (no max_tokens, no timestamp). Recorded max_tokens can only be inferred, e.g. predicted_n==2048 suggests a cap was hit. (advisor, replay-set, 2026-10-12)
- Each mem0 run's memory/mem0-history.db has tables memory_history and messages (bench/results/2026-10-12/m1-ngram/recon/inventory.json, mem0_dbs). memory_history uses mem0's history schema, not a `text` column. (advisor, replay-set, 2026-10-12)
- mem0 tap records include extraction calls triggered by the agent's mem0_memory add tool as well as the once-per-prompt auto-capture (site/series/memory-layers/mem0-in-pi.md:101-160), so each mem replay request needs its own new-messages content and per-call cutoff. (advisor, replay-set, 2026-10-12)
- mem0 extraction requests carry response_format {type: json_object} (mem0_extract_src.txt:866-870), so mem replay bodies must include it; it constrains decoding and may interact with speculation. (advisor, replay-set, 2026-10-12)
- recon/mem0_extract_src.txt is raw JS source: the full ADDITIVE_EXTRACTION_PROMPT is lines 11-486 (a second, truncated copy starts at line 615), and template-literal escapes (\\, \`, \uXXXX) must be decoded to get the runtime prompt text. (advisor, replay-set, 2026-10-12)
- pi's recorded thinking blocks carry thinkingSignature='reasoning_content' (recon/event_samples.json:457), and agent prompt growth after long-reasoning turns (e.g. baseline-r0/0/2 predicted_n=8565, then the recorded prompt goes 2761->13032 by turn 5) indicates that recorded agent prompts included earlier reasoning, so agent replay bodies that drop reasoning under-size the real traffic. (advisor, replay-set, 2026-10-12)
- Recorded agent prompts include earlier reasoning in full: in baseline-r0 step0 the recorded prompt grows 2761->13032 tokens from turn 2 to 5, which matches the 10165 tokens generated in turns 2-4 (inventory.json), and that generated text tokenizes at ~3 chars/token. So chars/4 under-counts reasoning-heavy agent prompts (replay_manifest.json baseline-r0/0/5). (advisor, replay-set, 2026-10-12)
- replay_manifest.json carries each request's recorded predicted_n, which ranges up to 8565 for agent (baseline-r0/0/2) and is 2048 for mem0-r0/2/0 (cap hit). Replay bodies have no max_tokens, so the probe must set the same per-request max_tokens in both arms, derived from predicted_n, or the decode tok/s and output-identity comparisons are invalid. (advisor, replay-set, 2026-10-12)
- The M1 mem replay set (replay_manifest.json) has 12 requests: 7 from mem0-r0 step0, none from mem0-r2. Each is ~1.03 est/recorded because the fixed ~33.6k-char ADDITIVE prompt dominates, so mem n-gram results mostly reflect that one shared system prompt. (advisor, replay-set, 2026-10-12)
- The llama.cpp-bonsai2 server only includes timings.draft_n/draft_n_accepted when n_draft_tokens > 0 (tools/server/server-common.cpp:82-85), so a missing field means 0 drafted, not missing data. (advisor, spec-replay, 2026-10-12)
- In off-greedy, the same request gives a different greedy output in single vs dual phases (requests.jsonl: baseline-r0/0/0 out_sha256 530c... vs 4694..., r0/0/8 predicted_n 141 vs 203), so temp-0 output depends on the batch mix; output identity between arms must be compared per phase, and dual-phase mismatches are expected without spec. (advisor, spec-replay, 2026-10-12)
- server-context.cpp:1172 'speculative decoding will use checkpoints' is logged with SRV_TRC and does not appear in replay logs at the default verbosity; use the 3813 'restore checkpoint' acceptance lines as evidence of checkpointed speculation. (advisor, spec-replay, 2026-10-12)
- A/greedy's single-agent 86.0 tok/s (bench/results/2026-10-12/m1-ngram/replay/A-greedy/requests.jsonl) is driven by two greedy loops that hit max_tokens (mem0-r0/0/2, mem0-r2/0/2) where spec-off finished normally with tool_calls. Without length rows A is about 54.3 tok/s vs off about 55, so ngram-mod defaults gave no speedup on normally finishing agent turns. (advisor, spec-replay, 2026-10-12)
- Enabling --spec-type ngram-mod changes temperature-0 outputs even with zero drafts: baseline-r0/0/0 single-agent out_sha256 is 530c... in off-greedy vs cdad... in A-greedy, both 71 tokens with draft_n 0, so off-vs-spec output identity cannot be assumed from lossless verification. (advisor, spec-replay, 2026-10-12)
- bench/spec_replay.py phase() records fg wall_s before stop.set()/th.join(), so bg tokens from the request in flight when fg ends complete outside that window; combined two-slot throughput must use a window that includes the bg join, or exclude bg rows that finished after fg ended. (advisor, spec-replay, 2026-10-12)
- bench/spec_analyze.py excludes the background request still in flight at foreground completion, so its combined figure avoids overcount but is a conservative completed-output throughput metric, not exact combined decode tok/s. (advisor, spec-replay, 2026-10-12)

  work if it has a memory layer, when everything (agent, memory, and embeddings) runs on
  a single RTX 3080?

  **Setup:** the [pi](https://github.com/badlogic/pi-mono) coding agent runs on
  Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B (a 2-bit, 27B model that fits in 6.7 GB). A mem0 memory layer
  uses the *same* weights through a second server slot, plus a small CPU embedder.

  **So far:**
  - Serving both roles from one copy of the weights works. Two parallel slots cost
    +150 MiB of VRAM and give about +45% aggregate throughput. A GPU scheduler change
    lets agent and memory requests run side by side.
  - First memory benchmark (1 task, 3 repeats): **mem0 finished the full 3-session
    sequence 2/3 times; no-memory baseline 0/3.** Memory carried facts and rules that
    were only ever *said*, never written into the repo.
  - N-gram self-speculation did **not** speed recorded agent or mem0 traffic with
    both slots busy, and changed outputs. It was not deployed.

  **Next ([roadmap](https://github.com/aiguy110/bonsai-garden/blob/main/docs/roadmap.md)):**
  more tasks and repeats, a guard that memory doesn't hurt unrelated tasks, and
  two other memory layers (agent-managed blocks, Graphiti) to compare with mem0.

    again, and a changed fact never replaces the old one.

    calls, but the agent has to decide what to save.
  - **Graphiti**, a temporal knowledge graph. Facts have validity intervals, so
    updates replace old facts, at the cost of several LLM calls per write.

tldr: A walk through the pi-memory-mem0 extension and mem0's write and search paths, with what our eval runs actually stored.
summary: |
  **What it is:** `@amaster.ai/pi-memory-mem0` 0.1.24, a pi extension that runs
  mem0 OSS 3.3.1 *inside* pi's process. All its LLM calls go to Bonsai's second
  slot (`bonsai-mem`), and embeddings come from a CPU server.

  **How it hooks in:** four pi events.
  - `input` remembers the prompt and starts a memory search in the background.
  - `before_agent_start` waits up to 3 s for the results and injects them as a
    user-channel message.
  - `turn_end` sends the prompt plus the **first** assistant reply with text to
    mem0.
  - `session_shutdown` waits for pending writes.

  The agent also gets a `mem0_memory` tool (search, add, list, delete).

  **What a write costs:** one LLM call with a ~36 KB system prompt, plus the 10
  nearest existing memories, plus the new messages. mem0 3.x only **adds**
  memories and skips exact duplicates. It never updates or deletes.

  **What we saw:** in the eval runs Bonsai used the tool on its own to save the
  conventions and the staging host. One run saved the same fact 4 times in
  different words, and the store kept 2 copies. The ~8k-token prompt was reused
  from cache in only 4 of 22 writes.

layer: experiment

title: Engine baseline and shared-weights options
status: done
date: 2026-10-10
updated: 2026-10-11
tldr: Measured decode at depth (~45 tok/s at 32k) and found that a second server slot, not a second model, is the way to give memory its own LLM.
summary: |
  **Question:** how fast is Bonsai-2-27B on an RTX 3080? And how can a memory
  layer get its "own" LLM without loading the weights twice?

  **Results:**
  - Single stream: prefill ~1170 tok/s and decode **64 tok/s** on an empty
    context. At 32k tokens of context, that falls to **~45 tok/s**. Use the
    second number when planning for agents.
  - q8_0 and q4_0 KV cache run at the same speed. q4_0 halves KV memory.
  - Batching several sequences on **one copy of the weights** scales well: 2
    sequences give 95 tok/s aggregate, 8 give 152.
  - Separate server processes would each load 6.7 GB onto the GPU, so that option
    is out. **One server with two slots** shares the weights, and each slot only
    uses the context its prompt needs.

  **Conclusion:** the memory LLM should be slot 1 of the agent's server. The GPU
  scheduler then becomes the bottleneck, because it admitted one request at a
  time. That set up the next two experiments.

===== site/series/serving/turnstile-coadmission.md =====
---
layer: experiment
series: serving
title: GPU scheduler co-admission and virtual models
status: done
date: 2026-10-11
updated: 2026-10-12
tldr: Turnstile now lets agent and memory requests run together on one model, with a context budget and per-role limits; all 9 live checks pass.
summary: |
  **Problem:** [turnstile](https://github.com/aiguy110/gpu-turnstile), the GPU scheduler shared by everything on this machine,
  admitted one LLM request at a time. It also evicted models by name. So memory
  calls had to wait behind the agent, and the two-slot speedup could never happen.

  **Change:** three features.
  1. **Co-admission:** a queued request can join running ones for the same model,
     up to its slot count. It never jumps ahead of higher-priority work.
  2. **Context budget:** concurrent requests must fit together in the server's
     shared 96k-token pool.
  3. **Virtual models:** `bonsai-agent` and `bonsai-mem` map to the real model.
     Each pins a slot, caps context, and can inject request settings, e.g.
     thinking off and temperature 0.2 for memory.

  **Validation (live, 9/9 pass):** agent and memory overlapped with **0 ms** wait,
  decoding at 44–45 tok/s each. Slot pinning held. Oversized requests got a clean
  400. Two 50k-token requests correctly took turns. GPU leases waited for both LLM
  requests to finish.

title: Two-slot server and prompt-cache behaviour
status: done
date: 2026-10-11
updated: 2026-10-11
tldr: Deployed the 2-slot server; replaying agent traffic showed every turn prefills only its new tokens, so the planned checkpoint tuning was unnecessary.
summary: |
  **Question:** does the two-slot config behave in production? And does the
  prompt cache force agents to re-process thousands of tokens each turn?

  **Why it mattered:** Bonsai is a hybrid model. Its recurrent layers can't be
  rewound, so if a new prompt diverges from the cached one, the server falls back
  to the last saved checkpoint. The default checkpoint spacing could mean ~8k
  tokens (~9 s) of re-prefill per agent turn.

  **Results:**
  - Deployed: 9503 MiB VRAM, 44.6 tok/s per stream with both slots busy.
  - A 14-turn tool-calling replay (to ~17k tokens) prefilled **only the new
    tokens each turn**. That held with the default spacing and with 4x denser
    checkpoints. This fork checkpoints right at the end of each prompt, so
    append-only traffic never rolls back. A real pi session looked the same.
  - Requests can be pinned to a slot (`id_slot`), and thinking can be turned off
    per request. The memory role needs both.

  **Conclusion:** no cache tuning shipped. The issue may come back once
  compaction starts rewriting history.
---

Decode rate is generated tokens divided by server-reported generation time. A
"combined" rate was also calculated from completed foreground output plus only
background requests that ended before the foreground ended. It is deliberately
conservative rather than an exact GPU rate. Its apparent A dual-agent advantage
(51.4 vs 47.8 tok/s) comes from different sampled output lengths: A completed
17,355 foreground and 21,359 eligible background tokens, versus 9,831 and
9,666 off. Per-request agent decode was slower, so this is not a speedup.

## Correctness and compatibility

Speculation materially changed output hashes: under production sampling, A
matched the no-speculation foreground hash on 4/30 single-agent requests, 10/12
single-memory, 0/30 dual-agent, and 9/12 dual-memory. Some variation is expected
from sampling and concurrent batching, but greedy decoding also changed with
speculation, including requests with zero drafted tokens. In one greedy
single-agent comparison A made two additional requests run to their token cap;
they normally finished with tool calls off-speculation. That is a quality risk,
not a throughput win.

The multimodal projector loaded and text-only requests did draft tokens; GPU
use was effectively unchanged (9507--9508 MiB with and without A). This does
not establish image compatibility. The server rejects a speculative batch that
carries image embeddings, so image traffic remains untested and risky with this
option.

## Decision

The deployment rule was a benefit while both slots are busy. Neither tested
setting met it, and default `ngram-mod` regressed both production two-slot
foreground roles. The live `bonsai-2-27b` entry is therefore unchanged. Raw
requests, server logs, VRAM samples, and replay notes are under
[`bench/results/2026-10-12/m1-ngram/replay/`](https://github.com/aiguy110/bonsai-garden/tree/main/bench/results/2026-10-12/m1-ngram/replay).

## 1. `--spec-type` — available values (from `help.txt`)

`--spec-type` selects the speculative-decoding backend. The value list:

```
--spec-type none,draft-simple,draft-eagle3,draft-mtp,draft-dflash,draft-dspark,ngram-simple,ngram-map-k,ngram-map-k4v,ngram-mod,ngram-cache
```

The **default is `none`** (no speculation). The **ngram family** is what M1
targets (self-speculation over n-grams of the current prompt, no separate
draft weights):

- `ngram-simple` — self-speculation over simple n-gram matches.
- `ngram-map-k`, `ngram-map-k4v` — n-gram map variants (k=1 vs k=4v).
- `ngram-mod` — the "mod" n-gram variant (probed in `docs/engine-review.md`; **not** present in the live entry, §1/§3).
- `ngram-cache` — n-gram with caching.

The **draft family** (`draft-simple`, `draft-eagle3`, `draft-mtp`,
`draft-dflash`, `draft-dspark`) requires a separate draft weights
file via `--spec-draft-model`. The current live entry (`serving/llama-swap.bonsai-2-27b.yaml`) carries **no** `--spec-*` flag, so it runs with the default `--spec-type none` (no speculation, §3).

=== m1-notes.md (rest) ===
replay probe will use on :8089, not what is live. Draft stats
(`timings.draft_n` / `timings.draft_n_accepted`) only appear when
speculation is on (see §3, §7).

## 3. spec + mmproj verdict: mmproj may load, but embedded image batches cannot speculate

`--mmproj` does not prevent initializing an n-gram backend, and this text-only
replay confirms it runs (`draft_n > 0`). This is not compatibility with image
traffic: `server-context.cpp:3550-3553` throws `unsupported batch.has_embd +
spec case` when a request batch carries embeddings. Thus speculation is usable
for these text-only replay requests, while image input with spec is untested and
risky. The initialization logic is:
`tools/server/server-context.cpp` is cross-checked against the recon's
`spec_lines_full.txt` (every line matching `speculative|spec`, numbered) and,
for lines that keyword-grep misses, against the host window `spec_ctx.txt`:
verified quotes below are literal.

- **`server-context.cpp:424-426`** — `can_speculate()` returns `!!spec`: the
  only gate is whether a spec backend object exists.
  ```
  424: bool can_speculate() const {
  425: return !!spec;
  426: }
  ```
- **`server-context.cpp:1123, 1128`** — the mmproj/multimodal block disables
  `ctx_shift` and `cache_reuse`; it does not prevent spec initialization.
  ```
  1123: SRV_WRN("%s\n", "ctx_shift is not supported by multimodal, it will be disabled");
  1128: SRV_WRN("%s\n", "cache_reuse is not supported by multimodal, it will be disabled");
  ```
- **`server-context.cpp:~1168`** — `speculative decoding not supported by
  this context` means sequence removal is unsupported and speculation was not
  initialized. The distinct checkpoint notice is at 1171-1172 (`speculative
  decoding will use checkpoints`) and is trace-level.
  ```
  1168: SRV_WRN("%s", "speculative decoding not supported by this context\n");
  ```
- **`server-context.cpp:1184-1191`** — spec init is gated on the context
  sequence-removal type only, with **no** mctx/mmproj term. From the host
  window `spec_ctx.txt` (literal):
  ```
  1184:         // try speculative decoding
  1185:         if (ctx_tgt_seq_rm_type != COMMON_CONTEXT_SEQ_RM_TYPE_NO) {
  1186:             try {
  1187:                 spec.reset(common_speculative_init(params_base.speculative, params_base.n_parallel));
  1188:             } catch (const std::exception & e) {
  1189:                 SRV_ERR("failed to initialize speculative decoding context: %s\n", e.what());
  1190:             }
  1191:         }
  ```
  `ctx_tgt_seq_rm_type` is set at 1166 from
  `common_context_can_seq_rm(ctx_tgt)` — also no multimodal condition.
- **`server-context.cpp:1212`** — every slot gets `slot.spec = spec.get()`
  regardless of mctx.
  ```
  1212: slot.spec    = spec.get();
  ```

**Verdict:** the production command with `--mmproj` loaded works for
text-only speculative replay: A/prod recorded 25,774 drafted and 5,954 accepted
tokens. Do not infer image compatibility from that result: batches with
`has_embd` hit the explicit unsupported spec case above. If a spec run has zero
drafts, look for `not supported by this context`; checkpointed acceptance is
instead evidenced by `accepted N/M draft tokens (restore checkpoint)` at 3813
(the 1172 checkpoint notice is trace-level and absent at default verbosity).

## 4. Message-reconstruction mapping (from `event_samples.json`)

The event schema is the canonical source for rebuilding the transcript.
Chosen step is `inventory-mem0-r2/step1` (8942 events, `n_distinct_types:
12`): `session, agent_start, turn_start, message_start, message_end,
message_update, tool_execution_start, tool_execution_update, tool_execution_end,
turn_end, agent_end, agent_settled`.

Confirmed from `event_samples.json` (this round):
- **The system prompt comes from a `role == "system"` message.** Both the
  `message_start.message` and `agent_end.messages[0]` entries have
  `role == "system"` and carry a `sections` map
  (`{preamble, tools, rules, docs, cwd}`). The `content` field is empty; the
  `sections` map *is* the payload. Sampled values:
    - `preamble` = `"You are an expert coding assistant operating insid..."`
    - `tools` = `"<tools>\n- read: Read file contents\n- bash: Execute..."`
    - `rules` = `"<rules>\n- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg..."`
    - `docs` = `"<docs>\nP i documentation (read only when the user a..."`
    - `cwd` = `"<cwd>\n/home/dev/inventory\n</cwd>"`
  Each non-`preamble` section is wrapped in a `<name>...</name>` tag
  (`preamble` is raw). This matches `buildSystemPromptSections(input)` in
  `dist/core/system-prompt.js`; `buildSystemPromptState` returns
  `{content: "", sections}` and `getSystemMessageText` (from
  `@earendil-works/pi-ai`) renders the sections into the final system-prompt
  text sent to the model.
- **`message_start.message.toolsAdded` exists.** It is a list of 5 tool
  schemas for the mem0 run: `read`, `bash`, `edit`, `write`, `mem0_memory`.
  Each tool has keys `name`, `description`, `parameters`
  (`{type, required, properties}`), and `constrainedSampling`
  (`{"type": "json_schema", "strict": "prefer"}`). These built-in pi tool
  schemas are dumped in full in `pi_prompt_src.txt` (from the chosen step in
  `event_samples.json`) — that is the exact tool list the agent prompt is
  built from.

Key mappings for reconstruction:
- **Transcript** → the `messages` array in `agent_end`
  (`{role, content, sections?}` per message). `agent_end.messages` reconstructs
  the whole conversation.
- **Assistant output** → `message_start`/`message_update` for
  `role == "assistant"`; `turn_end.message` carries the final assistant
  `content` (a list of `{type:"thinking", thinking, thinkingSignature}` and
  `{type:"toolCall", id, name, arguments}` blocks) plus per-message
  `usage`, `api` (`openai-completions`), `provider` (`garden`), `model`
  (`bonsai-agent`), `stopReason`, `responseId`, `responseModel`
  (the GGUF path), `rawStopReason`.
- **Tool calls** → `tool_execution_start` `{toolCallId, toolName, args}`;
  `tool_execution_update` / `tool_execution_end` carry progress/completion;
  `turn_end.toolResults` carries the per-call result
  (`{role:"toolResult", toolCallId, toolName, content, isError, timestamp}`),
  which is replayed as a tool-result message.
- **Usage/tokens** → `message_update.usage`
  (`{input, output, cacheRead, cacheWrite, totalTokens, cost}`), also
  present per message in `turn_end.message.usage`
  (`{input, output, cacheRead, cacheWrite, reasoning, totalTokens, cost}`).

---
layer: series
series: serving
order: 1
title: Serving two roles from one model on 10 GB
status: done
updated: 2026-10-12
tldr: One server with two slots runs the agent and the memory layer on a single copy of the weights; the GPU scheduler now lets them overlap.
summary: |
  **Goal:** run the agent and the memory layer's LLM on the same 27B model without
  a second copy of the weights. A second copy would need another 6.7 GB, and the GPU
  only has 10.

  **Findings:**
  - A single llama-server with **two parallel slots** shares one copy of the
    weights. The second slot costs about **+150 MiB**. Each stream drops from 61 to
    45 tok/s, but total throughput rises about **45%**.
  - At realistic agent context depth (32k tokens), decode is **~45 tok/s**, not the
    headline 64.
  - The prompt cache handles append-only agent conversations perfectly. Each turn
    prefills only the new tokens, so no tuning was needed.
  - The GPU scheduler ([turnstile](https://github.com/aiguy110/gpu-turnstile)) used to admit one request at a time, which
    erased the gain. It now co-admits up to `slots` requests for the same model,
    keeps a shared context budget, and exposes per-role virtual models
    (`bonsai-agent`, `bonsai-mem`). All 9 live validation checks pass.

  **Status:** deployed. A real-traffic replay found n-gram self-speculation
  slower when both slots are busy, so it was not deployed. Per-role KV-cache
  precision remains deferred until the memory evals show a need.
---

This series answers a feasibility question that comes before any memory
experiment: can both roles fit, and can they run at the same time?

## What carried forward

- The production config: `bonsai-2-27b` with `--parallel 2 --kv-unified -c 98304`,
  plus q4_0 KV.
- Two virtual model names in turnstile: `bonsai-agent` (pinned to slot 0, 80k
  context cap) and `bonsai-mem` (slot 1, 32k cap, thinking off, temperature 0.2).
- Planning number: ~45 tok/s decode per stream when both slots are busy or the
  context is deep.

## Deferred ideas

- **N-gram self-speculation (closed).** Despite its synthetic repeated-text
  result, it regressed real two-slot agent and memory replay traffic. The live
  entry remains without a `--spec-*` flag.
- **Different KV precision per role.** This needs a custom server. Only worth it
  if memory quality turns out to be sensitive to KV quantization.
